1:1: Paul was in prison because people in authority did not want him to preach about Jesus. They put him there in order to stop him and to punish him. This does not mean that Jesus had put Paul in prison.
Paul is using the term brother to mean someone who shares the same faith.
1:2: Paul is using the term sister to mean a woman who shares the same faith.

The letter is predominantly addressed to Philemon. It could be misleading to suggest Paul is writing to Apphia, Archippus, and the church in Philemon’s house, on the same level as he is writing to Philemon.
Archippus is the name of a man in the church with Philemon.
Paul speaks here of Archippus as if he and Archippus were both soldiers in an army. He means that Archippus works hard, as Paul himself works hard, to spread the gospel.
καὶ τῇ κατ’ οἶκόν σου ἐκκλησίᾳ
Apphia and Archippus were probably also members of the church that met at Philemon’s house.
1:3: After introducing the senders and recipients of the letter, Paul gives a blessing.
1:5: Paul is using a poetic structure here in which the first and last parts relate and the second and third parts relate.
1:6: Here, that introduces the content of the prayer that Paul mentions in verse 4.
1:7: Here, inward parts refers to a person’s emotions or inner being.
τὰ σπλάγχνα τῶν ἁγίων ἀναπέπαυται διὰ σοῦ
Here, being refreshed refers to the feeling of encouragement or relief.
Paul called Philemon brother because they were both believers, and he wanted to emphasize their friendship.
1:8: Here Paul begins his plea and the reason for his letter. Suggested heading: “Paul’s Request”
This could mean: (1) “all authority because of Christ”; (2) “all courage because of Christ.”
1:9: Paul was in prison because people in authority did not want him to preach about Jesus. They put him there in order to stop him and to punish him. This does not mean that Jesus had put Paul in prison.
1:10: Here, fathered is a metaphor that means that Onesimus became a believer as Paul taught him about Christ.
Prisoners were often bound in chains. Paul was in prison when he taught Onesimus and was still in prison when he wrote this letter.
1:12: Paul was probably sending Onesimus with another believer who carried this letter.
The phrase this one is my inward parts is a metaphor for deep feelings about someone. Paul was saying this about Onesimus.
Here, inward parts is figurative for the place of a person’s emotions. If not, use plain language.
1:13: Paul knows that Philemon wants to help him, and so he suggests that a way to do that would be to allow Onesimus to serve Paul in prison.
Prisoners were often bound in chains. Paul was in prison when he told Onesimus about the Messiah, and he was still in prison when he wrote this letter.
Paul was in prison because he preached the gospel publicly.
1:16: This does not mean that Onesimus will no longer be a slave to Philemon.
Here, brother is a metaphor for a fellow believer.
1:18: εἰ δέ τι ἠδίκησέν σε ἢ ὀφείλει
These two phrases mean similar things, although wronged you is more general than owes {you}.
1:19: ἐγὼ Παῦλος ἔγραψα τῇ ἐμῇ χειρί

Paul wrote this part with his own hand so that Philemon would know that these words were really from Paul, and that Paul really would pay him. He used the past tense here because the action of writing would be in the past when Philemon read the letter.
Paul says that he will not say something to Philemon while saying it. This is a polite way of emphasizing the truth of what Paul is telling him.

Paul was implying that whatever Onesimus or Paul owed to Philemon was canceled by the larger amount that Philemon owed to Paul, which was Philemon’s own life. The reason that Philemon owed Paul his life can be made explicit.
1:20: Here, brother is a metaphor for a fellow believer.
This metaphor refers to being a believer in Jesus and means the same as in Christ.
ἀνάπαυσόν μου τὰ σπλάγχνα ἐν Χριστῷ
How Paul wanted Philemon to refresh him can be made explicit.
Here, refresh is a metaphor for comfort or encourage.
Here, inward parts is a metonym for a person’s feelings, thoughts, or inner being.
1:21: Paul used the past tense here because the action of writing would be in the past when Philemon read the letter.
1:22: Here Paul closes his letter and gives final instruction to Philemon and a blessing on Philemon and on the believers that met for church in Philemon’s house. Suggested heading: “Final Instruction and Blessing”
The word translated guest room refers to any hospitality that is provided for a guest. So the kind of space is unspecified.
The words your and you here are plural, referring to Philemon and all the believers who met in his house.
1:23: Epaphras was the name of a man who was a fellow believer and prisoner with Paul.
Here, in Christ Jesus means something similar to the phrases “in the Lord” and “in Christ” in verse 20.
1:25: The words your spirit are a synecdoche and represent the people themselves. Paul is referring to Philemon and all who met in his house.
The word your here is plural and refers to Philemon and all who met in his house.
